blocks.title: Thermoregulation
blocks.text: Thermoregulation is a homeostasis in which organisms maintain their body temperature despite variations in the temperature of the environment.

High temperature denatures enzymes and damages metabolism. Plants use evaporative cooling to cope with heat, but hot, dry weather causes a shortage of water that closes the stomata, so plants suffer in such conditions. Most plants have adapted to survive heat stress, as the plants of temperate regions face temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius and higher. Their cells synthesise large quantities of special proteins, the heat-shock proteins, which embrace enzymes and other proteins and so help to prevent their denaturation.

Low temperature alters the fluidity of the cell membrane, because the membrane lipids become locked into crystalline structures, which affects the transport of solutes; the structure of membrane proteins is affected too. Plants respond to cold stress by increasing the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids, which help the membrane keep its structure at low temperature by preventing crystal formation. This adaptation takes time, which is why rapid chilling is more stressful than a gradual drop in air temperature.

Freezing temperatures cause ice crystals to form. If ice forms only around the cell wall the plant is not badly affected and survives, but ice crystals forming within the protoplasm perforate the membranes and organelles and kill the cells. Plants native to cold regions, such as oaks, maples and roses, have adapted by changing the solute composition of their cells, which lets the cytosol supercool without ice forming, although ice crystals may form in the cell walls.

blocks.caption: Adaptations to temperature stress
rows: Enzymes denature; stomata close in dry heat
Evaporative cooling; heat-shock proteins protect enzymes and other proteins
Membrane lipids crystallise, fluidity and transport fall; proteins affected
More unsaturated fatty acids in the membrane, built up gradually
Ice inside the protoplasm perforates membranes and organelles
Altered solutes let the cytosol supercool; ice confined to the cell walls

blocks.prompt: Why does a sudden frost kill a plant that would have survived the same temperature reached slowly?
blocks.explanation: Protecting membranes against cold needs time: the plant must raise the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids so the lipids do not crystallise, and adjust its solutes so the cytosol can supercool. A gradual fall allows this; a sudden chill does not, so membranes stiffen and ice may form inside the protoplasm and kill the cells.

items: Heat denatures enzymes; plants cool by evaporation and make heat-shock proteins that shield proteins from denaturation (temperate plants face 40 degrees and more).

Cold locks membrane lipids into crystals; plants add unsaturated fatty acids, slowly, so sudden chilling is worse. Freezing kills if ice forms inside the protoplasm; cold-region plants (oaks, maples, roses) change solutes so the cytosol supercools.
